extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (Kantian teleology), advanced readers studying the Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading/analysis of Kant's account of teleology in the Critique of Judgment, supplying the conceptual criteria for when teleological (purposive) talk is to be used regulatively or dogmatically and how human cognitive limits shape that use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dogmatic versus critical treatment of a concept
rubrics_metrics.description: “We deal with a concept dogmatically (even though it should be empirically conditioned) if we consider it as contained under another concept of the Object which constitutes a principle of Reason, and determine it in conformity with this. But we deal with it merely critically, if we consider it only in reference to our cognitive faculties ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dogmatic procedure is appropriate only when the objective reality of the concept is assured (so it can be constitutive for determinant judgements). If objective reality cannot be established, the concept must be treated critically — i.e. judged with regard to our cognitive faculties and only used regulatively. The text instructs readers to check whether objective reality can be proven before subsuming objects under a concept dogmatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of a thing as a natural purpose is regulative, not constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not constitutive for the determinant Judgement, but merely regulative for the reflective.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concept of natural purpose as a regulative maxim for reflective judgement (a guide for how we must apply our cognitive faculties), not as a constitutive principle that determines objects themselves. In practice this means one may adopt purposive conceptions to guide investigation of organisms, but cannot assert purposiveness as an objective property of things on the basis of reason alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective reality of purposiveness cannot be proven a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: “Therefore it cannot be dogmatically treated for the determinant Judgement ... it is not susceptible of proof through Reason as regards its objective reality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the concept of a natural purpose unites necessity (natural law) and contingency (form), its objective reality would require a ground beyond experience; this cannot be supplied a priori. Consequently, claims that natural purposiveness (or final causes) are objectively true cannot be established by reason alone, and any such dogmatic assertion is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological inference justifies a subjective (reflective) maxim, not a proof of God
rubrics_metrics.description: “Objectively we cannot therefore lay down the proposition, there is an intelligent original Being; but only subjectively, for the use of our Judgement in its reflection upon the purposes in nature ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleology provides a necessary maxim for human reflective judgement (we cannot think certain natural products except by representing them as if produced by design), but this does not amount to an objective theological proof. One may legitimately adopt the idea of a designing cause as a human heuristic, yet one must not present it as demonstrative proof that God exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt design-as-heuristic when investigating organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are in fact indispensably obliged to ascribe the concept of design to nature if we wish to investigate it, though only in its organised products ... this maxim of the reflective Judgement is essentially necessary.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When empirically studying organised (biological) entities, it is necessary and useful to employ purposive/concept-of-design thinking as a guiding rule to discover laws and internal constitutions. This use is methodological/regulative: it aids investigation though it does not settle metaphysical questions about objective designedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer actuality from mere conceivability (possibility ≠ actuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is indispensably necessary for the human Understanding to distinguish between the possibility and the actuality of things ... The distinction ... has merely subjective validity for the human Understanding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For human cognition, the fact that we can conceive a thing or represent it as possible does not justify concluding that it actually exists. This is a caution against deriving ontological claims from mere conceptual possibility; it underpins the critique of dogmatic teleological inferences that move from conceivable purposiveness to actual designers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason's Ideas are regulative, not constitutive, for cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reason ... contains in itself, as theoretical Reason, absolutely no constitutive but merely regulative principles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcendent Ideas (e.g., unconditioned ground, absolute purpose) must be treated as regulative maxims that structure inquiry rather than as constitutive concepts that determine objects. The Understanding supplies concepts and is required for objectivity; Reason furnishes ideals that guide the search for unity but do not themselves confer objective reality on objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human discursive understanding causes teleological representation of certain natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: Because our Understanding is discursive (a faculty of concepts proceeding from the universal to the particular) and the particular is contingent in many ways, “we represent products of nature as possible, according to a different kind of causality from that of the natural laws of matter, namely, that of purposes and final causes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contingency in how particulars accord with our universal concepts forces judgment to employ the idea of purposiveness; this is a feature of human cognition rather than an immediate property of nature. Recognize teleological descriptions as arising from the structure of our cognitive faculties (subsuming particulars under universals), not necessarily from the intrinsic constitution of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate of an intuitive (archetypal) Understanding as heuristic (intellectus archetypus)
rubrics_metrics.description: We may think an intuitive Understanding (intellectus archetypus) which proceeds from the synthetical-universal (the whole) to the particular, making the connexion of parts non-contingent and explaining purposive unity without requiring design attributed to parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce the idea of a higher or different kind of understanding as a heuristic to make sense of purposive unity (i.e., imagine an intellect that intuits wholes). Kant emphasizes that one need not prove such an intellect exists; the idea helps explain why we are led to teleological thought given our discursive mode of cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical explanation and teleological principle are compatible but distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: “The principle of a mechanical derivation of purposive natural products is consistent with the teleological, but in no way enables us to dispense with it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuing mechanical laws to explain biological form is necessary and legitimate, but mechanistic explanations do not render teleological judgement superfluous. Even with full mechanical knowledge, human judgement may still require teleological maxims to understand the unity of organised beings; both explanatory modes can be maintained without contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hylozoism or theism as dogmatic keys to teleology without first showing mechanistic insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hylozoism ... does not furnish what it promises.” And though Theism “rescues ... the purposiveness of nature from Idealism” it cannot dogmatically establish natural purposes; we must first prove the impossibility of the unity of purpose in matter resulting from mere mechanism before justifiedly placing the ground beyond nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dogmatically invoke hylozoism (life inherent in matter) or Theism to explain natural purposiveness unless one has, from the standpoint of permissible human judgement, shown that mechanistic accounts cannot in principle supply the unity required. The text warns against prematurely appealing to supernatural explanations.
